LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- Striking Hollywood writers will be back at their keyboards Wednesday after voting overwhelmingly to end a 100-day walkout that essentially shut down the entertainment industry. Writers Guild of America member Steven Binder shows his approval as he votes Tuesday in Beverly Hills, California. More than 92 percent of the Writers Guild of America members who cast ballots Tuesday in Los Angeles and New York voted to end their work stoppage over residuals for writing in the digital age, including new media and the Internet. The new deal is for three years. "The strike is over. Our membership has voted, and writers can go back to work," said Patric Verrone, president of the WGA's West chapter. Michael Winship, president of WGA's East guild, said, "The success of this strike is a significant achievement not only for ourselves but the entire creative community, now and in the future." WGA members walked off the job November 5 after talks broke down over how writers are paid for the use of their material on the Internet and DVDs, among other issues. "It is not all that we hoped for, and it is not all we deserve," Verrone said when a tentative deal was announced Saturday. But he added, "This is the best deal this guild has bargained for in 30 years." Leslie Moonves, chief executive officer of CBS Corp., told The Associated Press, "At the end of the day, everybody won. "It was a fair deal and one that the companies can live with, and it recognizes the large contribution that writers have made to the industry." The Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, which represents production companies and media conglomerates, has had no comment on the agreement. The vote meant that the Academy Awards ceremony on February 24 will be the usual scripted gala, the AP reported. "I am ecstatic that the 80th Academy Awards presentation can now proceed full steam ahead," without "hesitation or discomfort" for the nominees, Sid Ganis, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which stages the Oscars, told the AP. As long as the strike continued, the traditional Oscars spectacular was in doubt since many Hollywood stars would not cross WGA picket lines. It's unclear how soon new episodes of scripted programs will start appearing, because production won't begin until scripts are completed, the AP reported. It will take at least four weeks for producers to get the first post-strike episodes of comedies back on the air; dramas will take six to eight weeks, the AP said. Verrone said the WGA achieved two of three goals through negotiations with the studios.  Watch Verrone explain what he thinks the strike accomplished » . The first goal relates to writers' "jurisdiction" in new media, Verrone said, meaning that any content written by guild members specifically for new media, such as the Internet or cell phones, will be covered by their contract. The second goal relates to reuse of content in new media, Verrone said. The agreement bases payment for reuses on a distributor's gross formula for residuals, "so that when they get paid, we get paid," he said. It is the "first time in our history that a new delivery system pays on a residual formula superior to the prior existing system," Verrone said. The third goal, which Verrone said the guild did not achieve, was to shore up writers' shares of the revenue from animation and reality television. "Giving up animation and reality was a heartbreaking thing for me personally," he said. "But it was more important that we make a deal that benefited the membership, the town as a whole, that got people back to work and that solved the biggest problems in new media." LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Hollywood’s striking screenwriters are set to resume work Wednesday after decisively approving an end to a 100-day labor dispute that had brought much of the entertainment business to a standstill.

On Tuesday in Beverly Hills, California, Writers Guild of America member Steven Binder signaled his support while casting his vote. More than 92 percent of participating WGA members in Los Angeles and New York backed ending the walkout. The dispute centered on residual compensation for writing distributed through digital platforms, including the Internet and other new media. The resulting contract will remain in effect for three years.

Patric Verrone, head of the WGA’s western branch, announced that members had approved the agreement and were free to return to their jobs. Michael Winship, who leads the union’s eastern division, described the outcome as an important victory for both writers and the broader creative community, now and in years to come.

Guild members began their strike on November 5 after negotiations collapsed over several matters, including payment for material released online and on DVDs.

When the preliminary agreement was revealed Saturday, Verrone acknowledged that it did not provide everything writers had wanted or believed they were entitled to receive. Even so, he called it the strongest contract the guild had negotiated in three decades.

CBS Corp. chief executive Leslie Moonves told The Associated Press that, ultimately, all sides benefited. He characterized the settlement as equitable and acceptable to the companies while also recognizing writers’ major role in the entertainment industry.

The Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers, the organization representing studios, production businesses and large media corporations, did not comment on the agreement.

According to the AP, the vote also ensured that the February 24 Academy Awards would proceed as a conventional, fully scripted event. Sid Ganis, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences—the organization responsible for the Oscars—said he was thrilled that preparations for the 80th Academy Awards could move forward at full speed, without creating uncertainty or unease for nominees.

While the strike remained in effect, the usual Oscar spectacle had been uncertain because many Hollywood celebrities were unwilling to cross WGA picket lines.

The AP reported that the timing of new scripted television episodes remained unclear because production could not restart until scripts had been finished. Producers were expected to need at least four weeks to return comedies to television with post-strike episodes, while dramas would require approximately six to eight weeks.

Verrone said negotiations with the studios secured two of the guild’s three main objectives. In a video, he discussed what he believed the walkout had achieved.

The first objective involved WGA authority over new media. Under the agreement, the guild contract would apply to material created by its members specifically for platforms such as websites and mobile phones.

The second concerned compensation when content is reused through new media. Residual payments would be calculated using a formula tied to distributors’ gross revenue, meaning writers would receive compensation when distributors earned money. Verrone said this marked the first time in guild history that a new method of delivering content offered a residual-payment system better than the one already in place.

The guild did not accomplish its third objective: strengthening writers’ entitlement to revenue from reality television and animated productions. Verrone said abandoning those areas was personally painful. However, he believed reaching a settlement that helped guild members, supported the wider Hollywood community, returned people to work and addressed the most significant new-media concerns was more important.

The original report included an option to e-mail the story to a friend. Copyright 2008 CNN; all rights reserved. The material may not be republished, aired, rewritten or redistributed. The Associated Press contributed to the report.

outputs.L4:
Hollywood writers voted overwhelmingly to end their 100-day strike after union negotiators reached a tentative three-year contract with the major film and television studios. The walkout, organized by the Writers Guild of America, had halted production across the entertainment industry as writers sought better compensation and stronger protections for work distributed through digital downloads, Internet streaming and DVDs.

More than 92 percent of participating guild members approved a return to work, allowing writers to resume their jobs while the proposed contract proceeded through the formal ratification process. Guild leaders described the agreement as the union’s most significant advance in three decades.

A central issue in the dispute was how writers would be paid when movies and television programs were distributed through emerging digital platforms. The tentative deal established compensation for certain Internet downloads and streaming uses while expanding the guild’s jurisdiction over material created specifically for new media. Although union leaders acknowledged that the agreement did not achieve every objective, they said it created an important foundation for future negotiations as online distribution became increasingly important to the industry.

The strike had disrupted television schedules, delayed film projects and left thousands of writers and other production workers without work. Scripted series shortened or suspended their seasons, while late-night and other topical programs struggled to continue without their writing staffs.

Ending the walkout enabled studios and networks to restart production and helped the entertainment industry return to normal operations. It also removed uncertainty surrounding major events such as the Academy Awards, which could proceed with guild writers and without the threat of picketing that had affected other ceremonies during the strike.

Guild officials praised members for remaining united throughout the dispute, arguing that their solidarity had forced producers to address compensation for digital distribution. Writers returned to work with new contractual protections and a framework for sharing in revenues from the rapidly changing market for online entertainment.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened when the WGA voted on the tentative agreement ending the 2007–08 writers’ strike? Include vote totals, key quotes, contract terms, and the impact on the Oscars and television production.
counterfactuals.output:
On **February 12, 2008**, members of the Writers Guild of America voted overwhelmingly to end the 100-day strike and return to work under a tentative three-year agreement with the major studios.

### Vote and reaction

- **3,775 members voted to end the strike**
- **283 voted to continue it**
- Approval was approximately **92.5%**
- The strike officially ended at **12:01 a.m. on February 13, 2008**

WGA West president **Patric Verrone** described the agreement candidly:

> “It is not all that we hoped for, and it is not all that we deserve. But this is the best deal this guild has bargained for in 30 years.”

After the vote, the WGA announced:

> “The strike is over. Our membership has voted, and writers can go back to work.”

The union said it had secured its two central objectives:

> “Jurisdiction over new media and compensation for reuse on the Internet.”

The tentative agreement was later formally ratified by **93.6%** of voting members.

### Main contract terms

The three-year agreement gave writers, among other things:

- **WGA jurisdiction over qualifying original content made for the Internet and other new-media platforms**
- **Residual payments for ad-supported online streaming**, after an initial promotional window—generally 17 days, or 24 days for certain first-year series
- A movement toward a **percentage-of-distributor-gross formula** for later online reuse
- Improved compensation for **electronic sell-through**, such as paid downloads
- Guild coverage and minimum compensation for some higher-budget original new-media productions
- Restrictions and compensation rules governing the online use of film and television clips
- General minimum-pay increases over the contract’s three years

The writers did **not** win everything they sought. Most notably, the longstanding DVD residual formula was largely left unchanged, and some Internet terms included thresholds, windows and phase-ins that limited immediate payments.

### Effect on the Oscars

The settlement removed the threat of WGA picketing and allowed writers to prepare material for the **80th Academy Awards**, scheduled for **February 24, 2008**. Actors had indicated they would not cross a writers’ picket line, so an unresolved strike could have reduced the Oscars to something resembling the canceled press-conference version of that year’s Golden Globes.

Oscar producer **Gil Cates** said:

> “I am ecstatic that the 80th Academy Awards presentation can now proceed full steam ahead.”

The ceremony therefore went forward in its normal televised form, with host Jon Stewart and a full complement of presenters and nominees.

### Effect on television production

Writers returned to work immediately, but television did not instantly return to normal:

- **Late-night and comedy-variety programs** could restore their writing staffs quickly.
- Sitcoms and dramas reopened writers’ rooms and resumed production, but many produced only a **shortened batch of spring episodes**.
- Several series did not return until the following season because there was insufficient time to write and film additional episodes.
- The traditional **pilot season was badly compressed**, leading networks to order fewer pilots, rely more heavily on existing scripts and presentations, and make some decisions outside the usual schedule.
- Shows already in trouble were canceled or never restarted, while established series generally returned with reduced episode orders.

Thus, the vote ended the immediate labor stoppage and rescued major live events such as the Oscars, but the strike’s disruption continued to shape network schedules, episode counts and development practices for the remainder of 2008.
